S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.

subtypes.Initial Insomnia: Difficulty falling asleep and taking a long time to do so.
subtypes.Middle Insomnia: Waking up frequently during sleep or having difficulty falling back asleep.
subtypes.Early Morning Awakening: Waking up too early and being unable to fall back asleep.
subtypes.Hypersomnia: Sleeping for long periods at night or excessive sleep during the day.
subtypes.Nightmare Disorder: Sleep disturbance caused by repeated and distressing dreams.
subtypes.Non-Restorative Sleep: Feeling unrefreshed despite having slept enough.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).

subtypes.Fragmented Memory: Inability to recall only specific parts of the traumatic event while remembering others.
subtypes.Generalized Amnesia: Inability to recall the majority or the entirety of the traumatic event.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).

subtypes.Anhedonia for Happiness: Unable to feel happiness or joy even when good things happen.
subtypes.Lack of Satisfaction: Unable to experience satisfaction or pride even after achieving something good.
subtypes.Inability to Feel Love: Feeling numb to love or affection towards family or lovers.
subtypes.Emotional Numbness: A state where the mind feels empty and nothing is felt, as if all positive emotions are blocked.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.

subtypes.Scanning for Danger: Always scanning the surroundings and being alert to find potential threats or risks.
subtypes.Safety Checking: Repetitively confirming safety, such as checking exit locations or observing people around.
subtypes.Sustained Alertness: Unable to relax tension even in safe environments and maintaining a constant state of alertness.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is characterized by the development of anxiety, dissociative, and other stress-related symptoms within three days to one month following exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation. Core clinical features include intrusive recollections, avoidance, negative mood, dissociation, and marked arousal, with associated functional impairment. Symptoms must arise shortly after the trauma and resolve within a month; persistence beyond this period suggests possible progression to Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). ASD is distinguished from normative stress reactions by its severity, breadth of symptoms, and degree of interference with daily functioning, and from PTSD primarily by its shorter duration and greater emphasis on dissociative phenomena.

patient.personality: Mary is a methodical, community-focused operations manager who thrives on structured planning, data-heavy spreadsheets, and nurturing others while sometimes over-organizing to feel in control.
patient.stressor: On her way home from a late shift, Mary was driving through an intersection near her neighborhood when another car ran a red light at high speed and slammed into the vehicle in front of her, sending debris and glass across her lane and spinning the car onto the sidewalk where she had just been waiting at a previous light minutes earlier. She pulled over and, drawing on her natural tendency to take charge, called 911, directed bystanders, and stayed with an injured teenager in the crushed car until emergency services arrived, all the while acutely aware that she could easily have been in that position. Over the next several days, she tried to maintain her usual tightly scheduled routines at work and in her community volunteering, but found herself driving far out of her way to avoid the intersection, startling at sudden sounds in traffic, and feeling unable to fully relax even in familiar settings like her garden or church events, which began to affect her concentration and her willingness to drive to stores for her job. After about three weeks of feeling constantly tense on the road and noticing that her meticulous planning had escalated into excessive route-checking and avoidance that disrupted both work and family life, she decided to seek psychiatric help at her husband’s insistence when she started refusing to drive their children to activities.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since that crash, I’m on high alert all the time, especially when I’m out driving—it feels like danger is around every corner.”

S027.name: Sleep_Disturbance
S027.description: A state where there is a significant change in the quantity or quality of sleep.
S027.manifestation: Most nights I lie there for hours replaying the crash instead of falling asleep, and even when I finally drift off I jolt awake at every car that passes the house, so I never feel rested in the morning anymore.

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: Out of nowhere, even in the middle of a meeting or folding laundry, I’ll suddenly see that smashed car and the boy’s bloody face as if I’m standing there again, and my heart races and my hands start shaking like I’m back on the side of the road.

S071.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
S071.description: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event (typically due to dissociative amnesia and not to other factors like head injury or alcohol).
S071.manifestation: What’s strange is that there are whole chunks of that night I just can’t pull up—like I honestly don’t remember if I checked his breathing first or how long it took the ambulance to get there, even though I can picture other parts in sharp detail.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).
S076.manifestation: I keep going through the motions with my kids and my church group, but even when they’re laughing or I finish a big project at work, it’s like there’s a sheet of glass between me and the feeling—I know I should be happy, but it just doesn’t land.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: Lately the smallest things set me off, like my husband asking if I’m sure about the route I’m taking, and I’ll snap at him or bark at the kids for making noise in the car before I even realize how harsh I sound.

S079.name: Hypervigilance
S079.description: Persistent state of being alert and tense about the surrounding environment.
S079.manifestation: Whether I’m driving or just sitting in a pew at church, I catch myself constantly scanning for speeding cars, exits, and anything that looks off, and I can’t seem to let my guard down long enough to actually relax.
